title: Cadillac confirm Bottas will remain with the team in 2027
excerpt:
Cadillac have decided to stick with Valtteri Bottas for 2027, ending American Colton Herta's hopes of making his Formula 1 debut next season.

Bottas had signed a multi-year deal with Cadillac ahead of the American team's debut in the sport in 2026, but it required an option to be activated to trigger the second year.

The Finn has endured a difficult season, retiring nine times - only Aston Martin's Lance Stroll has failed to finish more with 13 DNFs - and his future was not mentioned when Cadillac announced a new multi-year deal for Sergio Perez in Mexico.

The American team were pondering their options, which included giving reserve driver Herta his F1 debut.

However, ahead of their third home race of the season in Las Vegas, Cadillac announced they were opting for "continuity and stability" by confirming Bottas for 2027, as they search for their first points in F1.

“To whom it may concern, I’m staying!” said Bottas. “I’m excited to continue this journey with Cadillac into 2027.

"We knew building a new Formula 1 team from the ground up wasn’t going to be easy, but that’s exactly what makes this challenge so special.

“We’ve laid the foundations, we’re learning and improving, and there’s still plenty more to come, I’m hungry for more, and I believe in what we’re building together. The story is only just getting started.”

CEO Dan Towriss added: “Valtteri’s experience, perspective and commitment are important strengths for our team.

"Continuity gives us a strong platform as we continue developing the team and working toward our ambitions in Formula 1.

"On the eve of the Las Vegas GP, everyone in the team is pleased to have Valtteri locked in for 2027 alongside Checo and look forward to the next stage of our journey together."

Cadillac said they will announce their reserve and test drivers "in due course".

The 2027 Formula 1 grid is almost complete, with just one seat at Haas left. That is set to go to incumbent Ollie Bearman once they complete contract talks.

title: Formula 1 and WHOOP announce landmark partnership
excerpt:
Formula 1 has today announced that WHOOP, the health and fitness wearable company, will join the sport as an Official Partner, to bring fans closer to the world-class athleticism required at the pinnacle of motorsport.

For more than 75 years, Formula 1 has showcased the world's greatest drivers pushing the limits of speed, skill and bravery. Through this groundbreaking partnership, utilising WHOOP's industry-leading wearable technology and combining it with the sport’s award-winning broadcast, fans will gain a deeper understanding into what the critical moments they witness over a Grand Prix weekend require both physically and mentally.

A cornerstone of the partnership will be the development of new broadcast storytelling experiences, featuring select insights delivered in the right way in collaboration with the drivers to provide fans with a real-time window into the physical realities of racing. These innovations will help showcase the human side of the sport in ways never seen before.

Fans will see the partnership brought to life across Formula 1's digital, social, and event platforms, as well as through trackside branding opportunities at races throughout the season.

WHOOP will also become an Official Partner of F1 ACADEMY, reinforcing a shared commitment to supporting and accelerating female talent in motorsport. Through the partnership, WHOOP and F1 ACADEMY will help showcase the performance, dedication and potential of the next generation of female racing drivers, while inspiring more women and girls to pursue opportunities both on and off the track.

The partnership reflects a shared commitment to understanding and celebrating human performance at the highest level. By combining Formula 1's global platform with WHOOP's expertise in performance insights, the collaboration will create new opportunities to connect our fans with some of the athletes at the centre of the sport.

Stefano Domenicali, President and CEO of Formula 1, said: “Formula 1 has always been about pushing boundaries, and this partnership with WHOOP opens up an incredibly exciting new chapter for our sport. For the first time we’ll be able to bring fans even closer to understanding what some of our drivers experience physically and mentally during the most intense moments of a race. The opportunity to uncover new insights, tell new stories and showcase the world-class athleticism that goes into making F1 one of the most extreme and exciting sports in the world, is truly groundbreaking. I can't wait to see these insights come to life through our broadcasts, giving fans a completely new way to experience Formula 1 while highlighting the incredible strength, resilience, and determination required to compete at the highest level of motorsport."

Will Ahmed, Founder and CEO of WHOOP, said: “WHOOP is bringing an entirely new dimension to Formula 1 by revealing the human performance behind the wheel. For decades, fans have had incredible insight into the cars, but less insight into the impact that races have on the drivers. Now, for the first time, we can show what happens inside a driver's body during the most intense moments of a race. This will change how fans experience Formula 1 and ultimately deepen our understanding of human performance.”

title: Why Russell won't run Mercedes' upgraded turbocharger in Vegas
excerpt:
Mercedes are set to launch their upgraded turbocharger at this weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix, but World Champion Kimi Antonelli is the only factory team driver set to run it.

The newly-crowned World Champions were permitted one upgrade on the power unit as part of the Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities (ADUO) mechanism.

They focused that work on their turbocharger and ahead of the Las Vegas Grand Prix, round 21 of the World Championship, the new part is ready for use by their factory team and customers, with rivals McLaren set to run it on both their cars.

Antonelli can take the new turbocharger without getting hit with a penalty, however his team mate George Russell has already used five of that part and thus would get a five-place penalty for the use of a sixth.

Following discussions internally, Mercedes do not feel it's worth taking the hit on Russell's starting position as they battle to help him secure second in the Drivers' Championship where he trails Max Verstappen by 17 points.

"This is primarily about proving out the development in race-weekend conditions, with the expected performance benefit relatively small," said Mercedes boss Toto Wolff.

"We anticipate running it with Kimi, whilst with George our priority is protecting his grid position with the performance benefit likely too limited to justify taking a grid penalty."

He added: "Our targets are clear: helping George finish as high as possible in the Drivers’ Championship, ending the year with momentum, and continuing to unlock more performance from the car.

"There is more work to do on that front, and the final three races give us three more opportunities to learn and improve."

Mercedes have won 12 times this season in the Grand Prix format, but their advantage over the field has reduced as the season has gone on - with just one of those wins coming in the last five rounds. This latest upgrade is just one of many steps to help them refine their 2027 project.

With both championships now sorted, after Antonelli became F1's youngest champion in Mexico with the team wrapping up their first Teams' Championship since 2021 last time out in Brazil, Mercedes' focus is on helping Russell take P2 and making sure the team are on a good foot for their title defences next year.

With three rounds still to go, Russell is very much in the fight for P2 as 33 points separate Verstappen, Russell, Lewis Hamilton, Charles Leclerc and Lando Norris with a maximum of 75 on the table.

Since the Las Vegas Grand Prix returned to the calendar in 2023, Mercedes have won once with Russell coming out on top in 2024.

title: How F1 drivers and strategists tackle the Las Vegas Grand Prix
excerpt:
Taking Formula 1 to Las Vegas is a headline-writer’s dream: Sin City is the place to go all-in, to roll the dice, to push the limits and risk it all… and it feels like the Grand Prix has caught a whiff of that too, with a circuit that offers low grip, unforgiving walls and plenty of overtaking opportunity for those prepared to gamble.

So how will the teams, drivers and strategists approach the weekend? It’s time to take a look in The Risk Perspective, in partnership with Marsh, Formula 1's Official Risk Partner and Official Insurance Brokering Partner.

The Set-Up

The F1 season has always enjoyed a mix of normal and oddball circuits, and while the modern eclectic calendar makes it hard to know what constitutes ‘normal’, Las Vegas is certainly out on the periphery of ‘oddball’, not because it’s a bumpy street track with very long straights, but because it’s very, very cold!

Racing in the high desert at night towards the end of November inevitably sees the mercury plunge and has teams reaching for the beanies, gilets and fingerless gloves that haven’t had an airing since winter testing in January. It provides the car with some power unit cooling for free, allowing it to run with tight bodywork and fewer shoulder louvres than usual.

Given the extreme temperatures at which the brakes of an F1 car operate, 10-20°C of ambient temperature doesn’t make much difference, but brake cooling is still a huge factor in Las Vegas, with the requirement being the opposite to most circuits, as the teams try to retain heat rather than reject it, potentially with seals on the brake drums.

The heat from the brakes is conducted into the wheels and used to warm the tyre carcasses, but it’s also valuable because of the length of the Strip Straight.

If the brake cooling is too effective, the cars arrive in the huge braking zone at T14 with cold brakes and no stopping power. There is, however, a balance to be achieved. Too much cooling and the cars struggle at the ends of the straights; too little and they overheat around the rest of the lap.

The big issue in these cold conditions is the potential for ‘graining’. This phenomenon is rubber tearing off the tyre surface in strips, and then immediately re-adhering to the surface of the tyre. It causes a significant reduction in grip and makes the cars very difficult to drive.

Sometimes this will simply be a phase the tyre goes through, with the grip returning once the surface has worn smooth again – but sometimes it doesn’t go away.

Avoiding – or limiting – graining is more art than science, usually aided by the driver introducing the tyre gently, rather than pushing too hard, too early, which leads to a tricky decision at the start of each stint, and a gamble between securing a position and looking after the long-term.

There are set-up tweaks that can help: the front-right has been the most susceptible tyre in Vegas, and so teams look to protect it with tweaks to lateral balance, and even by employing an asymmetrical set-up.

In terms of downforce, the length of the straights prompts teams to take downforce off the cars. The original belief with active aero was that F1 would stop producing the plethora of rear wings that characterised previous eras, but the empirical evidence is that designers still have some shots in the locker when it comes to rear wing type, and this weekend they’ll have the skinnier versions out.

That isn’t without risk, because taking downforce off the cars – on a track that’s inevitably going to have low grip already – is going to make them difficult to drive. But better this than being slow on the straights and a sitting duck when it comes to overtaking.

5 storylines we're excited about ahead of the Las Vegas GP

The Strategy: Guillaume Ducreux, Trackside Strategy Engineer, Racing Bulls

“Every track has its own characteristics, and in Las Vegas, the thing we’re very keen to understand is tyre graining. 2024 was heavily impacted by graining, which was the primary reason the race was two-stop. The graining was much-reduced in 2025 and without that limitation, the race was a one-stop.

“Obviously, for strategists, whether or not we have heavy graining in 2026 will be the main question to answer during practice. The long runs in FP2 should tell us what we can expect on Saturday night.

“Overall this year, we have not seen many instances, but we did see severe graining in Shanghai, all the way back in March. The significance of this comes from the fact the Chinese Grand Prix was impacted by low temperatures, and this weekend, racing at night in the desert, we’ll have temperatures that are likely even lower – and that could create the right conditions to see graining again.

“The last three years tell us this is a circuit where it is possible to overtake – but equally it’s also a race where track position is important. Being a street circuit, the chances of a Safety Car are high, and thus you want to have track position, want to be ahead, and thus limit your exposure to Safety Cars or red flags. That’s also a strong incentive to not box too early.

“Whether race pace or track position is more important really will depend on what sort of race we get. If it’s a two-stop, then race pace becomes more and more important, because you will have more opportunities during the race, whether that’s through undercuts or offsetting your stops [to build a tyre delta].

“Should we end-up with a one-stop race, obviously this moves the bias towards Qualifying pace and holding track position, because there will be fewer strategic opportunities. We could be in either scenario – it really will depend on how the tyres are behaving.”

The Drivers’ Perspective: Lando Norris

“It is certainly one of the hardest races of the year. There isn’t a lot of room for error – quite tricky and quite quick in terms of being a street circuit. There are white lines [on the asphalt], and all of that paint can be pretty horrible at times, when you’re in the car feeling these kinds of things. All in all, it will be a pretty insane challenge!

“Obviously, it’s cold, which is one of the biggest things, which leads to graining on the tyres, which is not always an easy thing to understand. We’ve had rain here, and it’s an incredibly difficult track in the rain – pretty nasty! And it won’t dry very quickly because of the temperature.”

The key section: Turn 12

For the sake of brevity it’s Turn 12, but the wonderful thing about racing in Las Vegas is that you’re never short of descriptions, so really it’s the junction of Sands Avenue and The Strip. There’s a high-speed section after The Sphere, following the twisting Sands Avenue past the Venetian, then a hard left onto The Strip by Treasure Island.

It’s a tight corner, approached at high speed on a bumpy section of track, and has seen plenty of cars locking-up and taking to the run-off – and in the case of Lando Norris in 2023, getting out of shape over the bumps and having a sizeable impact on the approach.

It's important, however, for more than just the potential to embarrass. Getting a good exit is crucial for performance all the way down the 1.9km straight that follows – and more so this year where it will impact energy deployment. Teams will therefore cant their set-up to ensuring the cars have good traction.

The Greatest Race: 2023 – A frenetic debut

The inaugural Las Vegas Grand Prix didn’t get off to the best of starts. First practice began at 2030 and ended approximately seven minutes later. A poorly-secured drain cover was pulled-up, damaging the cars of Esteban Ocon and Carlos Sainz.

The session was red-flagged and, as is the protocol in these situations, Race Control instituted checks on the welds of all the other drain covers which, on a street circuit measuring 6.2km, took quite a while. FP2 was delayed, leading to the bizarre spectacle of F1 cars still being on track shortly after 4am. Fortunately the race itself on Saturday evening was a fire-breathing monster.

The Ferraris had locked-out the front row but Sainz, as a result of his drain-cover related damage, also had a PU penalty to take, having ripped open the bottom of his car and damaged the Energy Store. He was relegated to P12, with Max Verstappen promoted to the front row.

Verstappen nipped through at the start to take the lead from Charles Leclerc, though he picked up a penalty for running off track. There was a VSC almost immediately to clear up damage from a collision down the field and a full Safety Car soon followed when Norris went off at the restart – providing a stark and early illustration of how the ultra-high speed circuit had real fangs.

Up top, there was a battle royale, with Leclerc harrying Verstappen and regaining the lead, before Verstappen dove into the pits for an early stop and to serve his penalty. Leclerc came in five laps later and the lead passed to Sergio Perez. The Mexican had started P11 and dropped to P18 at the start, before carving his way through the field.

Checo needed a bit of luck to properly get himself back into contention and it came via a collision between Verstappen and George Russell at T12, and a subsequent Safety Car required to clean up the debris. Russell picked up a penalty for that one.

Most of the field, including both Red Bulls, took advantage of the caution for a cheap stop, but crucially, Leclerc did not, and thus reassumed the lead of the race, which restarted on Lap 29 for 21 laps of high drama. Perez put a great move on Leclerc to recapture the lead on Lap 32, pulling out of the slipstream at the end of the Strip Straight. Leclerc took it back on 35 in the same spot.

Verstappen slipped past Perez on the next lap, then took the lead on Lap 37, and then Perez passed Leclerc when the Ferrari had a lock-up and when deep into T12 on Lap 43. The Red Bull 1-2 was not to last, however, with Leclerc staging a last lap, last-gasp recover to take P2 in the final braking point of the race and came home 0.171s ahead of Perez.

Breathtaking stuff, and the Las Vegas Grand Prix was off to a flier. The calamity of Thursday was largely forgotten, and F1’s return to Las Vegas was up and running with overwhelmingly positive vibes.

The Strategic Masterstroke: 2025 – Kimi rolls the dice

Last year, everyone did a one-stop… but not all one-stops are the same. Kimi Antonelli’s race stands out. He used an offset strategy to rise from P17 on the grid to P4 at the flag, which retrospectively became P3, and only passed two cars on track to do it.

It’d be notable for the sheer economy of effort alone… but it’s also worthy of note for reading conditions perfectly.

Antonelli started P17, ejected in the Q1 lottery as the track improved and times tumbled. With everyone improving on their final laps, he picked the wrong lap on which to have a lock-up, and was out.

The Mercedes W16, however, had decent pace – and Kimi just needed some clean air in which to use it. He was the only driver to start the race on the desperately-unfancied soft compound, and indeed, the only driver to use it in the race.

The intention was clearly a short, sharp, opening burst, then an early stop, hoping to undercut cars ahead. An early VSC, however, made that opening stint very short and very sharp, with the Mercedes driver pitting on Lap 2, and doing the rest of the race on the hard compound.

Antonelli rose to P14 on the first lap, dropping to P15 with his stop. Stopping under a VSC had a pit-loss time of 13.5s versus 20s for a green flag stop, and thus he gained considerable virtual ground, passing cars as they pitted ahead and came out behind.

While the hard was robust, completing 48 laps required very careful management, and Antonelli and his engineering group had to hold their nerve to push through a period of graining in the middle of the race, waiting for it to clean-up, rather than pitting for a second set of hards.

“Kimi had a great race considering his start position,” said Andrew Shovlin, Mercedes’ Trackside Engineering Director.

“We knew starting on the soft and stopping early was a risk but if the hard tyre held on to the finish, it was our best chance to get him into good points. We took the opportunity presented by the early Virtual Safety Car and from there he drove brilliantly to keep his tyres in good shape, whilst making some critical overtakes.”

The Risk Perspective is brought to you in association with Marsh, Formula 1’s Official Risk Partner and Official Insurance Brokering Partner.

title: Breaking: Cadillac make crucial F1 driver announcement ahead of Las Vegas GP
excerpt:
Valtteri Bottas will remain with Cadillac for the 2027 Formula 1 season, the American team has confirmed.

The announcement gives the squad continuity as it builds on its maiden campaign on the grid. It forms part of Cadillac's long-term ambition to establish itself as a competitive force at the top of the sport.

Bottas brings considerable Formula 1 experience, technical insight and race-winning pedigree to the team. His feedback and leadership are set to continue supporting the squad's development across its operations in Silverstone, Indianapolis and Charlotte.

"To whom it may concern, I'm staying!" said Bottas.

"I'm excited to continue this journey with Cadillac into 2027. We knew building a new Formula 1 team from the ground up wasn't going to be easy, but that's exactly what makes this challenge so special.

"We've laid the foundations, we're learning and improving, and there's still plenty more to come, I'm hungry for more, and I believe in what we're building together. The story is only just getting started."

Cadillac CEO Dan Towriss also welcomed the news, with the team currently preparing for this weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix.

"Valtteri's experience, perspective and commitment are important strengths for our team," said Towriss.

"Continuity gives us a strong platform as we continue developing the team and working toward our ambitions in Formula 1.

"On the eve of the Las Vegas GP, everyone in the team is pleased to have Valtteri locked in for 2027 alongside Checo and look forward to the next stage of our journey together."

Reserve and test drivers for the squad are set to be announced in due course.

title: Fernando Alonso drops out as Aston Martin make Las Vegas GP FP1 driver change
excerpt:
Aston Martin has confirmed that Jak Crawford will take over Fernando Alonso's AMR26 for the first practice session at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

The outing will see the American third driver make his F1 practice debut on home soil on Thursday. It will be the 21-year-old's fifth FP1 appearance of the campaign with the Silverstone-based outfit.

Crawford has now covered more than 4800 kilometres in Formula 1 machinery, experience the team says continues to sharpen his technical feedback and development work.

"I'm really looking forward to getting back behind the wheel of the AMR26 in Las Vegas," said Crawford.

"It's particularly special to be doing it in the US, and I'm excited to get out on track in front of the American fans.

"My session in Mexico City finished earlier than planned, so it's great to have another opportunity to get behind the wheel again so soon.

"I'll be focused on making the most of the session and providing useful feedback to help the team prepare for the weekend."

title: Liam Lawson 'curious' as F1 personal driver data to be shown live with new deal
excerpt:
A new spotlight is about to open up on a previously unseen aspect of the drivers on track exploits.

18 November 8:06PM

F1 has unveiled a new deal with wearable health and fitness giant Whoop that will broadcast the personal data of several drivers live during a grand prix.

Liam Lawson, confirmed last week as a Racing Bulls driver for next season, is the first F1 face of a device he has regularly used, but which will now play an instrumental role in training, sleep, and other key lifestyle aspects of his career.

Whoop has joined forces with F1 in a four-year agreement that will shed a spotlight on an aspect of the sport so far unseen.

Will Ahmed, founder and CEO of Whoop, speaking to select media, including RacingNews365, in Las Vegas, said: "Millions of data points come off the car, but historically, very little data has been coming off the driver, and so we're excited to change that.

"We're going to be able to broadcast live physiological data from a driver in the car to the overall broadcast that fans are watching at home, and this will include pieces of information like live heart rate and zones of maximum heart rate, being able to show how much stress a driver is experiencing in real time.

"We have a stress monitor, which is an understanding of someone's live heart rate variability, which is this lens into their autonomic nervous system. So that'll be a component of it.

"Over time, we're going to be looking at trends around sleep and recovery, and seeing how some of that data affects the performance of the drivers. This is all going to be done in conjunction with the participating drivers and with their consent.

"But we want to be able to tell a big story about how incredible what these guys do really is. It's worth saying that the data we're producing for these drivers will also go to them and the teams themselves.

"So there should be a whole research component and scientific component for the teams around performance, which is to say, how gruelling is one race versus another? What was the preparation going into that race, and how did it affect the driver?

"Are there things we can shift about the travel schedule, the training schedule, the lead-up to the race, about our preparation that can make the driver more successful?"

[Article continues below]

Driver

Liam Lawson

New Zealander

30

Domenicali - 'We are missing an important element'

The data of Lawson and other drivers who have, as yet, not been named will be broadcast from early next season.

F1 CEO and president Stefano Domenicali has described the partnership with Whoop as "something totally new, very fascinating".

He added: "Our sport is full of data, and sometimes we are missing an important element of it, which is the performance of our drivers, who are fantastic, unique.

"Doing this together, we can open a different way of living races for people who are interested in understanding the level of performance of their heroes.

"It is up to us to create the right tool, to translate all the data we have into something easy to understand, attractive and interesting. We're gonna have an incredible winter to prepare all this stuff."

Lawson joked that his Whoop device would at least show him "going into the last few races trying to relax a little bit more" because prior to the eventual confirmation of his new deal, the last few months had "been pretty stressful".

Looking ahead to wearing the app in-race, he said: "A lot goes into a Formula 1 race and what we're feeling, and what people see on TV is us racing all the time.

"But there are a lot of things that you go through when you're racing, whether it's a red flag, a restart, something like this, or just the start of the race when you're in a close fight with another car, when you're in a qualifying lap.

"Depending on what's really going on, we're still human. We stress about things that are not just driving, so it's cool for people to be able to see that."

[Article continues below]

Lawson - 'It's not just watching the cars drive around'

Lawson claims he will be "quite curious" to see the broadcast data of his F1 rivals, noting that "you will probably get to see some of the guys who maybe train a little bit harder than others, how they're feeling in a race."

The New Zealander added: "I think that the most interesting part, at least for me, is that I will find out more and more that people are really, really interested in these details. It's not just watching the cars drive around.

"Over the years, obviously, the access that people get into our backgrounds, our lives and stuff like that is very interesting. People really seem to like that.

"So I feel like seeing the sort of different emotions that you go through... a race is very, very long. Our sport is definitely on the endurance side of things.

"So yeah, the different levels of stress that you go through in a race, even on a lap, the different parts of the lap; if you're on a really high-speed track, you're pulling a lot of g-force, it's hard to breathe.

"So, those sections of the track are a lot more physical, and it will show people that.

"It's going to be very interesting for people. For us, I'm curious as well to see what everybody else is doing."

title: Carlos Sainz sounds F1 alarm over 'counterproductive' growth
excerpt:
Carlos Sainz is worried by what the number of races on the F1 calendar might mean for the future of the sport.

Carlos Sainz has warned F1 that it could be “counterproductive” to have so many grands prix staged across the course of a season.

Over the last handful of years, F1 has steadily been increasing the number of race events, with 24 rounds now commonplace on the calendar.

With the sprint format featuring at 10 rounds next year, F1 fans will access more racing action than ever before.

However, Sainz has suggested that fans could be burned out by having so much in a condensed period of time.

“If I were a fan, I would love it because the more F1 I can watch on TV, the better,” Sainz told media including RacingNews365.

“I remember when I was a kid and there were only 16 races in the calendar, or 18. I used to miss Formula 1 for a lot of weekends.

“We also need to consider as a sport if that's something that maybe is also counterproductive. Sometimes you need to miss the sport to get people engaged.”

[Article continues below]

Driver

Carlos Sainz

Spanish

55

Sainz points to Champions League, Premier League comparison

F1 has seen a boom in popularity in recent years, which in turn has seen more locations around the world wanting a spot on the calendar.

The sport has suggested that 24 is the maximum it will have due to the constraints it would place on those who travel to each event.

Sainz stated F1 could be damaging its own atmosphere by having such an onslaught of events.

“When maybe you get so many races in a row, people or the sport can maybe feel a bit like a league, like the Premier League rather than the Champions League.

“So maybe you pay a bit less attention to the matches or to the races in this case.

“So, it's more a philosophy for the sport to consider whether you want to keep having so many races in a row.”

title: Liam Lawson wary of potential 'trouble' striking Las Vegas F1 grand prix
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has predicted "trouble" could arise at the Las Vegas Grand Prix if wet weather strikes after concerns over the tyres.

Last time out at the Sao Paulo GP, both qualifying and most of the race were held in wet conditions as the intermediate and full wet tyres were used in competition for the first time at length.

Feedback was largely negative from drivers as they felt the tyres could not retain heat and temperature to allow them to push.

This is despite Interlagos featuring a number of corners which allow for energy to be transferred through the tyre - something not present at the Las Vegas Strip Circuit, with its uber-long straights and low energy, slow-speed corners.

As such, with the cold air and track temperatures expected in Sin City, should it rain, as it could do in Thursday's two practice sessions and as it did during qualifying in 2025, Racing Bulls' Lawson predicted "trouble" could arise.

"Quite tricky," Lawson replied when asked by media, including RacingNews365, what his verdict was on the intermediate and wet tyres.

"The biggest problem [on Sunday in São Paulo] was the temperature was much cooler than [Saturday], and so even there there was less water; like on the laps to the grid, the cars were nearly undrivable, and the temps were going down.

"But at points where it rains a lot, it is not the standing water which is too much; it is that you can't actually keep temperature [in the tyres].

"So if we're at a track like Las Vegas and it rains, honestly, I think we're in trouble."

title: Expensive fiasco in Las Vegas results in worst F1 track - Throwback
excerpt:
Formula 1 returns to Las Vegas this weekend for the fourth running of the race on the Strip, a glitzy, high-speed showcase built around the city's famous boulevard.

But this is not the first time F1 has landed in Sin City, known as such for its casinos, nightlife and quickie weddings.

The previous attempt, more than four decades ago, is remembered for what is considered one of the worst circuits in the championship's history.

Some venues earn their place on the calendar and stick around. Others never win hearts at all.

Modern tracks such as Miami, Madrid and Abu Dhabi draw plenty of criticism, but none of them come close to the lows Formula 1 reached in the past.

Zeltweg, AVUS, Dallas, Nivelles-Baulers, and Las Vegas all rank among F1's least-loved layouts.

Not the Las Vegas Strip Circuit that has hosted the race since 2023, but its predecessor: the Caesars Palace Circuit.

Anyone familiar with Las Vegas will know Caesars Palace as a hotel and casino. It would be reasonable to assume the circuit wound through the streets around the building. It did not. The track was laid out entirely on the casino's car park and an adjoining stretch of vacant land.

[Article continues below]

Money talks

How did Formula 1 end up racing around a car park? The answer lies in a mix of financial and political factors.

For years, Watkins Glen had hosted the season finale, but the circuit ran into money troubles and could no longer meet modern safety requirements. It dropped off the calendar after 1980.

A replacement was needed, ideally one with the financial muscle to cover the steep cost of staging a grand prix.

Caesars Palace saw an opportunity, partly to polish its image and partly to lure wealthy visitors to the resort and its casino floor.

The original plan was for cars to race along parts of the Strip itself, much as they do today. That idea was dropped because Caesars Palace did not want to hand a promotional boost to rival casinos nearby.

Instead, organisers settled on the large car park behind the hotel, together with some adjacent open ground. A layout was drawn up, and the temporary circuit was built.

[Article continues below]

© Yoyodu10 via Wikimedia Commons

A grey, featureless loop

What could possibly go wrong? This was Las Vegas, after all, and the hosts were not shy about spending money to make a spectacle of it.

Yet the Caesars Palace Grand Prix was doomed almost from the start, and it duly flopped.

The first problem was the layout itself. A car park does not make an iconic circuit, and this one certainly was not.

The track was flat as a pancake and utterly uninspired, little more than a string of near-identical corners joined by two straights, all set against a grey concrete backdrop.

The races were also held in the early afternoon, in blistering heat. To make matters worse, the circuit ran anticlockwise, against the direction most tracks favoured at the time.

Drivers suffered badly for it, battling physical discomfort, nausea, and in some cases fainting behind the wheel.

[Article continues below]

Title deciders

Was there anything that made the race worth watching? As it happens, yes, though it had nothing to do with the circuit itself.

Both editions of the Caesars Palace Grand Prix doubled as the championship decider.

In 1981, it was a genuine three-way fight between Carlos Reutemann, Nelson Piquet and Jacques Laffite. With 49, 48 and 43 points respectively, all three still had a shot at the title.

Reutemann held the strongest hand, starting from pole, with Piquet fourth and Laffite down in eleventh.

But Reutemann's Williams developed gearbox and handling problems during the race, and he slid steadily backwards through the field.

The Argentine finished eighth, outside the points. Piquet had no great race either, but a fifth place was just enough.

By a single point, 50 to 49, Max Verstappen's father-in-law claimed the first of his three world championships.

[Article continues below]

The worst ever?

A year later, the title was settled in Las Vegas again. This time three drivers were still theoretically in contention: Keke Rosberg on 42 points, Didier Pironi on 39, and John Watson on 33.

Pironi was absent, having broken both legs in a horror crash earlier in the season that ended his career.

That left Rosberg and Watson to fight it out. Watson needed victory and a scoreless day for Rosberg. Neither happened.

Watson finished second, Rosberg fifth, and the Finn became the first from his country to win the F1 drivers' championship, arguably one of the most unexpected champions the sport has produced.

Those title fights were not enough to save the Caesars Palace Circuit's reputation.

More than four decades on, it is still widely regarded as perhaps the worst circuit Formula 1 has ever used, a dubious distinction unlikely to be taken from it any time soon.

Thankfully, Formula 1 now races on the Strip itself. The current Las Vegas circuit is far from a textbook classic, but it remains a vast improvement on what came before.

title: McLaren address Mercedes partnership for next F1 power unit regulations
excerpt:
McLaren has no plans to design its own power unit for Formula 1's next engine regulations, according to CEO Zak Brown, who says the Woking-based squad remains fully committed to its Mercedes customer relationship.

The topic has gained fresh relevance with F1, the FIA and manufacturers pushing to introduce a 2.1-litre turbocharged V8 formula from 2030, a year earlier than originally planned under the current cycle.

McLaren has run as a Mercedes High Performance Powertrains customer since the start of the current regulations and is contracted to continue doing so through 2030, alongside fellow customers Williams and Alpine.

Brown's comments come after McLaren endured early reliability issues in 2026, including hybrid battery problems that contributed to a double no-show in China, and after the team previously acknowledged a calibration knowledge gap compared to the factory Mercedes operation.

Asked whether McLaren was considering building its own power unit, Brown told the Sky F1 podcast there was no such plan in motion.

"There's no plan," said Brown. "You know, it's something that we look at. We're very happy with Mercedes HPP; they've been a great partner. We won two championships. I think we debunked the 'you can't win a championship with a customer engine' argument, so I think people don't need to kind of worry about that anymore.

"I think the challenge is, you can do what Red Bull did, well done. You can also be where Aston Martin is right now, so I'm just not sure the risk is worth the reward when we can win championships with Mercedes.

"Some of these challenges we had at the start of the year, if you had your own engine... But then if you get it wrong...

"So, I think with the V8s being pulled forward to 2030, which is what it looks like, I also think that, whether we wanted to or not, I don't think there's enough time to get ready. So, I think it's a watching brief, but at this point we have no plan."

Brown's reference to Aston Martin points to the Silverstone-based outfit's well-documented struggles since switching to a works Honda power unit this season, with packaging and vibration issues severely restricting its early-season running.

Red Bull, by contrast, successfully launched its own in-house engine project with Ford backing for 2026.

title: Formula E testing red flag carnage continues as Jake Dennis loses crucial running
excerpt:
The second day of Formula E pre-season testing saw mixed conditions across the day, with Edoardo Mortara and Jean-Eric Vergne topping the two sessions, respectively.

2023 Formula E world champion Jake Dennis suffered the biggest crash of pre-season testing so far on what was a crazy second day of testing in Madrid.

The second day of track action featured a dry morning but a mixed-conditions afternoon, with Turn 3 again causing chaos and being the main spot for red-flag carnage.

Edoardo Mortara was quickest on Wednesday morning in what was a fully dry session, unlike the afternoon. His 1m 24.496s was the fastest lap of Day 2, with a shower affecting the afternoon session.

Citroën's Jean-Eric Vergne topped the afternoon session, although lap times remained in the mid-1m 25s as the track dried late on.

The day featured five red flags, two fewer than Monday's total, taking the week's overall tally to 12. Dennis crashed in the morning at Turn 3 and lost four hours of running as a result.

Morning session

The opening session on the second day – the third session of the test in total – was another one dominated by red flags.

Paul Aron crashed at Turn 3 for Fortescue just 20 minutes into the session, ending his running for the morning. A spell of solid running followed before three more red flags in the final 50 minutes.

Lola's Robert Shwartzman came to a halt before Dennis' damaging crash at Turn 3, destroying the right-front of his Andretti. Stoffel Vandoorne's stoppage in the closing minutes saw the three hours of running end under red-flag conditions.

On the timesheets, Mahindra's Mortara was quickest again, although one-tenth shy of his 1m 24.3s set on Monday afternoon. Formula E's so-called 'test' driver Taylor Barnard was second.

Felipe Drugovich in third was also within two-tenths, while Opel's Mitch Evans and Nissan's Zane Maloney completed the top five.

CHECK OUT THE FULL MORNING RESULTS

Afternoon session

The afternoon running started with a mock E-Prix, although six drivers did not take part. Wet weather persisted throughout, with a large number of drivers not completing the full distance. Porsche and Opel looked strongest.

Mortara's trip into the gravel, which triggered a safety car, was the only real skirmish, with the mixed conditions offering teams a great data-gathering opportunity.

With two hours remaining, regular running resumed on a damp surface. As a result, lap times were well down on the best of the test so far. Nevertheless, the Gen4's performance remained impressive in the tricky conditions.

The afternoon almost ended under the 12th red flag of testing, caused by Shwartzman becoming the latest Turn 3 victim. However, running resumed with two minutes remaining.

Vergne set a 1m 25.437s in the closing seconds to top the session, ahead of Drugovich and Mortara. Stoffel Vandoorne, Enzo Fittipaldi and Dennis did not feature.

title: Everything still to be decided in final three races of 2026 F1 season
excerpt:
RacingNews365 takes a look at everything still to be decided in the final three rounds of the 2026 F1 season, starting in Las Vegas.

18 November 4:30PM

Both F1 championships are secure, but there is still plenty to be decided in the final three grands prix of 2026.

Kimi Antonelli and Mercedes will receive the top prizes in December, but behind them, there is still much that Las Vegas, Qatar, and Abu Dhabi will provide answers to - with millions of dollars in prize money on the line...

The headline act

In the drivers' standings, the headline outstanding matter is who will take the silver and bronze positions behind Kimi Antonelli.

As it stands, heading to Las Vegas this weekend, the advantage is currently in Max Verstappen's favour after his recent strong run of form.

The Dutch driver currently holds 279 points, with Mercedes' George Russell hoping to complete the perfect season for the team by taking second in the drivers'.

Russell has 262 points in third place, with Lewis Hamilton lurking just one point behind his former Mercedes team-mate.

Charles Leclerc (249) and Lando Norris (246) are also still in the mix, although catching Russell for third is likelier for both, with Leclerc 30 points behind Verstappen in second, and Norris 33 adrift.

The top three in the championship are required to attend the FIA prize-giving gala in Shanghai in the week after the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix.

[Article continues below]

© XPB Images

Elsewhere in the drivers'

In the remainder of the drivers' championship, there is a battle to finish inside the top 10.

As it stands, the battle looks to be between Pierre Gasly of Alpine and Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad.

Frenchman Gasly holds 42 points at the time of writing, with Lindblad on 38 in his rookie season.

Gasly could, in theory, finish ninth in the standings, but he is 47 points Liam Lawson, who holds 89, meaning this is unlikely, as is Franco Colapinto climbing up from his current haul of 27.

Meanwhile, honours at Audi are up for grabs, with both Gabriel Bortoleto and Nico Hulkenberg tied on 14 points apiece, with the Brazilian ahead on countback, with three eighth places to Hulkenberg's two.

There is also the Battle of Spain, with both Fernando Alonso and Carlos Sainz tied on seven points apiece.

Alonso's eighth place in Bahrain in Malaysia gives him the current dint over Sainz, whose best result in a poor season for Williams has been a trio of ninth places in China, Miami, and Canada.

Finally, in the race to avoid the wooden spoon, Lance Stroll, Valtteri Bottas, Sergio Perez, and Rafael Camara are wanting a strong result.

The best the quartet have finished this season is 12th for Stroll in Bahrain, 13th for Bottas in China, and 14th for Perez on three occasions.

Camara will be taking his second race in Las Vegas, although it is unclear whether he will try to win the F2 title in Qatar or Abu Dhabi or take the extra two F1 races.

[Article continues below]

© XPB Images

The constructors' fights

In the constructors', although every position bar Mercedes is still up for grabs, we have focused on the realistic fights, each worth millions of dollars in prize money.

Chief among them is the battle for third in the standings.

At present, Red Bull holds the place on 415 points, following its resurgence since the Azerbaijan GP, with Verstappen winning three times and taking two seconds, a third, and the Sprint win in Singapore.

It has overhauled McLaren, which has 398 points as it tries to rescue third place in its final three races as the defending world champions.

Ferrari is second, 90 points clear of Red Bull.

Racing Bulls are almost certainly going to finish in fifth, with 114 points to Alpine's 69 in sixth.

In seventh, another battle is brewing with Haas on 31 points ahead by just three of Audi's 28, although all three remaining circuits are not the strongest for either, with the power blasts in Vegas, Qatar, and Abu Dhabi requiring strong power units, something both squads lack. However, the Audi chassis is strong, which could be a trump card.

In the fight for ninth, Williams is currently on 12 points, ahead of Aston Martin on seven.

Finally, Cadillac will be hoping to finally score its first point of the season, and avoid becoming the first squad since Haas in 2021 to record a duck.

title: Kimi Antonelli rival rejects 'impatient' claim after rapid F1 title success
excerpt:
Gabriel Bortoleto has rejected claims that old F2 rival Kimi Antonelli's F1 title glory has made him "impatient" for glory of his own.

Antonelli became the youngest-ever F1 champion at the Mexico City Grand Prix, winning the title at 20 years, 2 months, 7 days old, and eclipsed Sebastian Vettel's record from 2010 of 23 years, 4 months, 11 days.

Antonelli, who is the third Italian to be champion, and first since Alberto Ascari in 1953, now holds the record by 3 years, 2 months, 4 days, but was defeated by Audi racer Bortoleto in their 2024 FIA F2 campaign.

Bortoleto claimed the championship that year and finished 101.5 points clear of Antonelli, with both graduating to F1 for 2025 - Antonelli with Mercedes and Bortoleto with Stake, which became Audi for '26.

Whilst Antonelli has roared to title glory, Audi and Bortoleto are continuing to build up their project, with the Brazilian banking points on debut in Australia, with the team slowly moving up to become regular points contenders in the upper midfield.

Reacting to whether Antonelli's glory had made him "impatient", Bortoleto firmly rejected the notion.

"Does it make me impatient? No, it doesn't make me impatient," Bortoleto explained to media, including RacingNews365.

"I would say it makes me even hungrier to achieve my goals, but I know we are on different journeys.

"Kimi is an incredible talent, and he has shown this in F1 and in junior series as well, and he has had a very good season, and he deserves to be world champion.

"Obviously, I want to achieve my goals as soon as I can, but as I mentioned, we are on different journeys, and when we joined his team, it was a team already fighting at the top.

"When I joined this team, we were a team that had just finished last in the constructors', so I knew the work we had to do, and I think we're going in the right direction.

"We have been improving our position, and now we are one of the top teams in the midfield, and we know where we need to improve.

"We have a few problems here and there, but we are always chasing that improvement, and hopefully, in the future, I can soon be fighting for titles, and hopefully with Kimi."

title: How Red Bull holds vital advantage over rivals at F1's toughest test
excerpt:
Red Bull is the team to beat at the Las Vegas Grand Prix. RacingNews365 technical analyst Paolo Filisetti explains why.

Formula 1 has headed to Las Vegas, one of the most unusual venues on the calendar, to kick off the season-ending triple header with Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

The Las Vegas Strip Circuit blends tight corners typical of a street track with some of the longest, fastest straights of the season, but the cold temperatures from the Mojave Desert nights are what make it a true outlier and arguably the most difficult weekend on the schedule.

The run from the start line to Turn 1 is short before drivers hit a tight 180-degree left-hander, followed by a very long right-hander where high downforce is essential. The first sector ends with the track's second-longest straight, leading into a 90-degree right-hander.

The middle sector is the most technical of the lap and the one where chassis and suspension quality matter most.

Turn 6 mirrors the characteristics of Turns 3 and 4, a long corner that loads the car with heavy lateral g-forces. That is followed by a tight chicane where getting the car onto the kerb cleanly is difficult, before another sharp left-hander on the exit. That exit is crucial, as it fires drivers into a high-speed section.

The second sector closes at Turn 12, where cars are launched onto the Strip itself. The final complex, Turns 14 to 16, includes a chicane that demands real care under braking to avoid locking up.

Out of Turn 16, drivers tackle the last straight before a flat-out corner leads back to the start-finish line.

The biggest challenge of the Las Vegas Grand Prix will be energy management. An additional complication comes from the very low ambient temperatures, as mentioned, which make it difficult to get the tyres up to temperature. Forecasts for qualifying and the 50-lap race are around 12 degrees Celsius.

[Article continues below]

Who is favourite and why?

Red Bull head to Las Vegas as the team to beat. The long straight and fast corners tend to play to the strengths of the RB22, which is welcome news for Max Verstappen and Isack Hadjar, who are driving the most improved package of the F1 season.

Verstappen has already shown strong form on this circuit in the past, and although the car is less suited to the middle sector, the Dutchman should be able to make up ground in the first and third sectors.

Mercedes, meanwhile, arrive as winners of both championships, but will not be the outright favourite.

The development of the W17 has not delivered the expected gains. Even so, the layout appears to suit the car, and energy management looks set to be its real strength.

Ferrari could struggle with the high top speeds reached on the straights in Las Vegas. The Scuderia should be competitive through the technical middle sector, but may pay a price on the long straights due to a power deficit from its power unit.

The low temperatures also make tyre warm-up tricky. The strong form shown in Mexico was largely down to the thin air at altitude there, which allowed the Italian engine to match its rivals on energy management, a factor that will not apply this weekend.

McLaren arrive fresh from a third win of the season in Brazil, but that result came on a track where the MCL40's notably draggy characteristics were not a handicap.

While the Mercedes power unit fitted to the car is an asset on the straights, the car's limited aerodynamic efficiency and short wheelbase look set to work against it in Las Vegas.

title: Frigid Las Vegas to present F1 drivers with most unique 2026 challenge
excerpt:
The Las Vegas Grand Prix this weekend will be unlike anything F1 drivers have experienced thus far in 2026.

Although the car systems are well understood as we approach Round 21 of 23, the conditions in Nevada promise to be a real head-scratcher.

The two complicating factors are the cold climatic conditions and the very layout of the Strip circuit itself.

The mercury is not forecast to get above 10-15 degrees Celsius all weekend in Nevada when the cars are on-track, with Las Vegas noticeably colder during the night than the day.

This is because there is often little cloud cover in Sin City at night, meaning heat cannot be trapped in as it burns off beneath the clear skies, with the desert also a poor heat trapper.

As such, with the cold air and track conditions, the tyres cool down.

This is then exacerbated by the very nature of the track itself.

With its long straights, including the long blast down the Strip, the tyres cool down as they are not being worked to generate temperature. Following this, there are no high-speed changes of direction on the circuit, such as the Esses at Suzuka or Maggots and Beckets at Silverstone, to force energy and heat through the tyre to generate temperature.

With this lack of opportunities to force heat into the compound with the high number of low-speed corners, the tyres then cool further, meaning it becomes a vicious circle as drivers cannot generate heat as they have so little grip - and because they have so little grip, they cannot push to generate temperature.

Another, additional complication in 2026 is the power units.

With their 50:50 split in power output between the ICE and the batteries, it means on long straights, cars slow down as the battery drains.

This means at the left-right-left chicane at the end of the Strip before the turn for home, cars will be arriving even slower than in previous years - thus with less energy, which makes it harder to generate temperature.

[Article continues below]

But all is not bad

On the flip side, the low-energy, low-heat demands placed on the tyres mean that degradation and wear are seldom encountered in Las Vegas.

This means drivers are able to push flat out on their tyres during stints, with a one-stop flat-out blast expected around the 50 laps, in conditions similar to Azerbaijan.

With tyre warm-up expected to be difficult, drivers are likely to complete multiple warm-up and prep laps in qualifying, as opposed to a single out-lap before attempting a flying lap.

For the race, it means that an overcut, where a car stays out for longer as it has tyre temperature, is likely to be effective over the usual undercut.

title: Max Verstappen raises 'different behaviours' warning ahead of unique F1 challenge
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has warned that the cold could shake up the order at this weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix, where teams face the twin demands of keeping heat in their tyres and managing battery deployment on the Strip.

Air temperatures are expected to be around 12-13°C for Friday's qualifying session and the start of Saturday's race, both of which get underway at 8pm local time. That makes the November night race one of the coldest tests on the F1 calendar.

The long straights give tyres time to cool before drivers reach the braking zones, while the shortage of fast corners leaves few opportunities to build that heat back up.

A car that gets its tyres working on a single preparation lap could gain places in qualifying over rivals whose drivers are still searching for grip into the first corner.

Those same straights put a premium on how teams use the electrical power available each lap. A driver who uses more battery power on the exit onto the Strip may have less in reserve towards the end of the straight, leaving an opportunity for a rival who has saved some charge.

"Heading to Vegas, it is such a different track; it is a fast circuit and has the long straight, so the energy deployment and management will be a factor," Verstappen said.

"It is also cold, so we will see different tyre behaviours on different cars, and it will be important to manage these properly."

Red Bull head into the final three rounds third in the constructors' championship, 17 points clear of McLaren.

Verstappen is defending second in the drivers' standings behind champion Kimi Antonelli, with George Russell 17 points adrift and Lewis Hamilton a further point back.

He added: "We have made some really positive steps over the past few races: hopefully we can finish the season on a high going into the final few races before the end of the season and contribute as many points to the constructors' championship as we can."

title: 2026 F1 Las Vegas Grand Prix weather forecast
excerpt:
F1 drivers are to be met with typically cold conditions for this weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Current forecasts for Sin City predict around 10 to 14 degrees Celsius throughout the on-track action, which is due to the local climatic conditions.

With clear skies at night, heat is not trapped by clouds, with the desert sand located around Nevada also not retaining the heat of the day.

Unlike in 2025, when rain hit qualifying, it is not expected to disrupt the weekend - or is snow.

As of 11:00 GMT on Wednesday, November 18th, a huge storm system is making its way in from the Pacific Ocean into the contiguous United States, bringing severe rain and snow conditions.

However, as this huge system moves inland from west to east, it is forecast to run into the Rocky Mountains - which will dissipate it - and deflect the remnants north, away from Nevada and Las Vegas.

The trailing bottom edge could hit Las Vegas during Thursday evening's two practice sessions, but won't have an impact on qualifying or the race.

Behind this, another system is currently moving down from the Bering Sea and Gulf of Alaska, but this won't make landfall until Saturday evening on the west coast, near San Francisco, meaning it won't impact the grand prix, due for a 20:00 local time start on Saturday, November 21st.

As for the wind direction, for qualifying and the race, light winds are expected from the west, corresponding to a headwind on the final straight and kink to the start/finish line, which runs directly west.

It means it will be a crosswind on the Las Vegas Strip from left to right as the driver looks, although the impact of the winds will be minimal, owing to the number of buildings breaking up gusts.

title: 2027 Formula E pre-season testing - Madrid Day 2 morning results
excerpt:
Check out the full results from the second day morning session of Formula E's 2027 pre-season test, held in Madrid at the Circuito del Jarama.

Edoardo Mortara topped the morning session on the second day of Formula E pre-season testing in Madrid, as red flags flew once again.

It was yet another session featuring several red flags, with Paul Aron crashing just 20 minutes into the session at Turn 3.

Smooth running followed until the final hour, with Robert Shwartzman stopping and Jake Dennis also crashing at Turn 3 happening within just a few minutes of each other. Jaguar's Stoffel Vandoorne stopped in the final seconds, causing the session to end under a red flag. The overall testing red flag total has risen to 11 as a result.

Fusion's 'test' driver Taylor Barnard was second and 0.161s adrift of Mortara's 1m 24.496, with Felipe Drugovich, Mitch Evans and Zane Maloney completing the top five.
